Damian Paletta
 
Tillis Wants Hegseth Fired. Is the Pentagon Chief in Trouble?
 
Plus, the U.S.’s nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia includes a road map for enriching uranium, and the odd political alliance opposing data centers
 
 
KEVIN DIETSCH/GETTY IMAGES
 

Good morning. The aftershocks of Army Secretary Dan Driscoll’s resignation this week continue to rumble.

 

On Wednesday, Sen. Thom Tillis (R., N.C.) called for President Trump to replace Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The retiring senator’s critique of the Pentagon chief was harsh.

 

“I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country,” Tillis wrote of Hegseth. “He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force.”

 

“Ginning?” “Soberly?” Those are pretty loaded comments at a defense secretary who was once heavily criticized for his drinking.

 

To be sure, Hegseth is doing his job in a much different way than past Pentagon leaders. He posts videos of himself working out and trolls both adversaries and allies. He has ousted plenty of top military brass and tried to change the culture at the Defense Department.

 

His supporters, which notably include Trump, think Hegseth’s bravado is long overdue. And he does have support of many members in the military. But he is alienating plenty of people too, including many civilian and military leaders who are close to Republicans.

 

He has weathered storms before. But the new one forming looks to be getting bigger.

 

This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

Ted Cruz: The Texas senator wants to run for president again and is taking digs at Vice President JD Vance, the presumptive front-runner.

 

Trump’s Thursday: The president receives an intelligence briefing this morning, then will have policy meetings this afternoon. Vance will give a press briefing at 1 p.m. ET.

What I’m Following

 
 
LUIS SANTANA/TAMPA BAY TIMES/ZUMA PRESS
 

A new team has formed in the fight against data centers: Bernie Sanders, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and…Steve Bannon? The odd political alliance shows that AI is the latest horseshoe issue uniting the left and right populist flanks of each party. Bannon said he was looking past his disagreements with progressives on issues such as immigration because AI will be the defining issue of the future: “If we don’t get this right, none of that other stuff is going to matter.”

 

The Pentagon is quietly extending troop deployments in the Middle East. Hegseth’s all-in approach is part of an open-ended military strategy designed to give Trump options in the war, according to people familiar with the matter. But the deployment of 19 warships, air-defense units, fighter squadrons and paratroopers across the region is straining servicemembers and their families, and creating a maintenance backlog that could take years to unwind.

 

The Trump administration’s nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia includes a road map to enrich uranium. New details of the agreement to provide the kingdom with a civilian nuclear program showed how uranium might be enriched there. Congress is currently considering the deal, which has spurred criticism that it doesn’t do enough to prevent the risk of nuclear proliferation.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• Trump’s Venezuela oil grab is no quick fix for gas prices.

 

• Tech execs and administration officials urged policymakers from other countries to minimize AI regulations.

 

• Washington’s “Economic D-Day” against Iran faces steep odds.

 

• The U.S. is annoyed with China’s overreliance on exports for growth, and other countries agree.
